overview: Brent crude surged 3.1% to $116.70 on Friday, extending its rally to a fresh five-month high after Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its Dhahran headquarters following repeated Houthi drone attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. WTI rose 3.9% to $103.30, settling above $100 for a second consecutive session. Libya added to supply fears with a pipeline shutdown that cut production at two fields feeding the Zawya export terminal. Twenty-eight ships have now been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in October — a record — with 11 VLCCs damaged, about 3.5% of the global supertanker fleet. Crude flows through the strait remain above 12 million barrels a day but daily volumes continue to swing wildly. ING called its earlier $80 Q4 Brent forecast 'unattainable' and warned of renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf. Newcastle coal held near $151.

Gold broke below $4,000 for the first time this month, falling 0.7% to $3,995 as oil-driven inflation pressure kept the 10-year Treasury yield pinned at 5.2% ahead of the October 28 FOMC decision. Silver dropped 1.3% to $53.78, platinum dipped to $1,548, and palladium fell to $1,028. Copper bucked the metals selloff, rising 1.6% to $6.47 per pound on escalating Hormuz-related supply-chain concerns. Grains were mixed: December corn slipped 4½ cents to $4.56, November soybeans firmed 3½ cents to $12.56½ on export demand, and December wheat held at $6.25. Bitcoin drifted to $80,700 as risk appetite continued to ebb ahead of the FOMC, while Ethereum edged down to $2,375.

watchItems.title: FOMC decision, Oct 28
watchItems.text: The Fed meets Tuesday with the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.2% — its highest since 2007 — and Brent crude at $116.70. Gold's break below $4,000 suggests the market is pricing in a more hawkish stance. September CPI at 3.7% and oil's relentless climb complicate the committee's options. Markets still price 89–94% odds of a December hike.

watchItems.title: Oil approaching $120 as supply disruptions widen
watchItems.text: Brent has gained roughly 12% in two weeks, closing Friday at $116.70. Saudi Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters, Libya shut a pipeline feeding the Zawya terminal, and ING scrapped its $80 Q4 Brent forecast. Morgan Stanley expects global fuel markets to stay tight through mid-2027. US diesel hit $6.30 a gallon as the administration tapped the Northeast heating oil reserve.

watchItems.title: Hormuz attacks hit record 28 in October
watchItems.text: The Washington Institute counted 28 confirmed or reported attacks in October and 113 since the conflict began February 28. Eleven VLCCs have been damaged this month — about 3.5% of the global fleet. Shipowners keep loading inside the Gulf, attracted by daily freight rates above $1 million and steep discounts to dated Brent, putting more tonnage at risk. UKMTO says underreporting means the actual figure is higher.

watchItems.title: Iran escalating ahead of US midterm elections
watchItems.text: Analyst Noam Raydan says Iran is intensifying Hormuz attacks to slow the recovery in shipments and pressure global energy markets before November's US midterm elections. Reuters cited two senior Iranian officials confirming the tactic. A second US carrier deployment and reports of possible fresh strikes on Iran add to the risk of a wider escalation that could push Brent above $120.

desk.name: Gold
desk.sum: Gold fell 0.7% to $3,995 on Friday, breaking below the $4,000 level for the first time this month as oil's relentless surge kept the 10-year Treasury yield pinned at 5.2%. The dollar held firm near 101.6, adding to headwinds for the metal ahead of the October 28 FOMC decision. Gold is now roughly 29% below its January record near $5,608.

desk.name: Silver
desk.sum: Silver dropped 1.3% to $53.78 on Friday, extending losses as elevated real yields and a firm dollar weighed on the metal. Silver is down about 15% on the month and tracking its worst monthly performance since July. The gold-silver ratio held near 74, reflecting silver's underperformance relative to gold.

desk.name: Oil
desk.sum: Brent surged 3.1% to $116.70, a fresh five-month high, after Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its Dhahran headquarters following Houthi drone attacks. WTI rose 3.9% to $103.30, settling above $100 for a second day. Libya's pipeline shutdown cut output at two fields feeding the Zawya terminal, adding to supply fears. ING called its $80 Q4 Brent forecast 'unattainable.'

desk.name: Copper
desk.sum: Copper rebounded 1.6% to $6.47 per pound on Friday, bucking the broader metals weakness as escalating Hormuz disruption threatened Middle East sulfur supply chains critical to copper processing. The metal remains about 5.5% below its September high of $6.85 and down roughly 4.6% on the month.

desk.name: Coal
desk.sum: Newcastle coal edged down 0.3% to $150.70 on Friday, holding near its highest levels since late 2024 as oil's surge overshadowed the coal complex. The IEA forecasts record global coal demand of 8.94 billion tonnes this year as the Hormuz gas shock drives Asian and European utilities back to coal. Indonesia's tighter export restrictions are adding to supply-side tightness.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.sum: Platinum slipped 0.7% to $1,548 on Friday, continuing its grind lower as elevated yields and a firm dollar suppressed the precious metals complex. The metal is down about 12% on the month and continues to underperform gold. The WPIC's forecast of an 18% drop in total platinum demand this year weighs on sentiment.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.sum: Palladium fell 0.8% to $1,028, extending its decline to the lowest level since mid-2025. The metal is now down about 22% over four weeks and more than 30% lower on the year. EV adoption continues to erode catalytic-converter demand, and Russia's sanctions waiver keeps Norilsk supply flowing.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.sum: Crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain above 12 million barrels a day, roughly 70% of the pre-war 17.1 million baseline, as US Navy convoys continue routing tankers along the Omani coast. However, October has seen a record 28 ship attacks with 11 VLCCs damaged — about 3.5% of the global supertanker fleet. Daily freight rates above $1 million are luring shipowners to load inside the Gulf despite the risk. Aramco's Dhahran HQ evacuation and a second US carrier deployment signal further escalation.

desk.name: Corn
desk.sum: December corn fell 4½ cents to $4.56 on Friday, pressured by harvest progress in dry weather. The US corn harvest is running near the five-year average pace. Corn is down about 16% on the month as fund liquidation and harvest pressure persist.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.sum: December wheat held at $6.25 on Friday, up a quarter cent, as the market found a floor after weeks of harvest-driven selling. Winter wheat planting is advancing and export demand remains subdued. Wheat is down about 14% on the month but remains more than 25% higher year-to-date on war-related supply concerns.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.sum: November soybeans firmed 3½ cents to $12.56½ on Friday, supported by continued Chinese import demand. Export sales rose sharply this week. The US harvest continues to run ahead of the five-year average, pointing to a record crop, but demand-side strength is providing a floor.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.sum: Bitcoin drifted lower to about $80,700 on Friday, falling 0.7% as risk appetite continued to ebb ahead of the October 28 FOMC. The $80,000 level is emerging as key support, with traders watching $79,500 below and $83,000 as the trigger for a trend reversal. Ethereum edged down 0.6% to $2,375. The broader crypto market remains subdued as oil-driven inflation fears dominate sentiment.

desk.name: LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) held near $29 per MMBtu, up roughly 12% on the week, as Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Qatar's 106 million tonnes a year of export capacity. European TTF trades near $28.9, its highest level since 2022. European gas prices are being driven higher by restricted Qatari LNG supply and winter demand. Henry Hub at $3.10 remains disconnected from global spot markets.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.sum: Sulfur prices remain elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,100–1,300 a tonne. Middle East FOB prices sit at $765 (Kuwait) and $740 (Qatar). China imported 56% of its sulfur from the Middle East pre-war, and Hormuz disruption continues squeezing sulfuric acid supply — the essential input for copper leaching, phosphate fertilizer, and oil refining. Domestic China sulfur trades near 7,200 yuan a tonne.

desk.name: Potash
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367.50 a tonne, down from $396.50 in July, as the market stays well supplied. China's 2025 contract settled at $348 a tonne. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions, routing through non-aligned buyers. Argus notes potash demand is expected to remain firm in 2026.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) held near 92,000 yuan a tonne as of mid-October, down 12.4% on the week from the post-holiday high of 105,000 yuan. China controls about 48% of global mine output and 80% of smelting. Military demand (ammunition hardener, flame retardants, night-vision optics) keeps the strategic premium high even as post-holiday demand disappoints. China's antimony oxide exports fell in September.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.sum: Gallium remains at a record $1,850 a kilogram outside China, up over 200% since early 2025. Beijing's Document No. 46 export controls set a presumption of denial for gallium exports to US end users. The Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspended that presumption for one year but Chinese exports have not meaningfully resumed. China produces about 98% of global gallium and 60% of germanium. Western recycling and new mines in Canada and Japan are years from meaningful output.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) averaged about $5.02 a pound in 2025, slipping from $5.44 in 2024 as steel demand softened. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage — cheaper per cycle than lithium-ion at 4+ hour durations. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. A single large VRFB order can move the market.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.sum: ICE cocoa edged up 0.3% to about $5,605 a tonne on Friday, stabilising after recent declines. The market remains historically extreme — it hit $12,931 in December 2024 — but prices have roughly halved from their peak as Ivory Coast arrivals improve and European grindings fall. Inventories are recovering but remain tight, and any weather scare across West Africa's cocoa belt can trigger a sharp reversal.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.sum: Cobalt metal traded around $56,108 a tonne on the Rotterdam spot market, with the DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintaining export quotas of 96,600 tonnes a year to support prices. LME cobalt sits lower near $33,000. The EV battery chemistry shift from nickel-cobalt (NMC) to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is structurally reducing cobalt demand, but aerospace and superalloy uses provide a floor.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures fell below 97,000 yuan a tonne (~$13,400), breaching the psychologically important 100,000 yuan level as oversupply overwhelms EV demand growth. The contract is now down about 24% on the month and roughly half its mid-May peak above 200,000 yuan. Australian spodumene miners continue cutting output below $1,000 a tonne. Institutions are warning of further oversupply into 2027.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades around $2,400 a tonne ($2.40/kg), firming on tight supply from Southeast Asia where Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia produce 70% of the world's latex. Fungal leaf blight (Pestalotiopsis) continues to reduce yields across the region. Auto-sector demand remains solid, and tyre makers are rebuilding inventories after destocking in 2024. SHFE rubber futures have climbed steadily through 2026.
